claims.text: Selective dealloying of a multi-element noble-metal high-entropy alloy can produce a three-dimensional nanoframework.
Dealloying preferentially etches the less noble constituents of the alloy.
Preferential etching leaves behind a porous, noble-metal-rich network.
The porous, noble-metal-rich network enhances catalytic properties.
The proposed starting material is a bulk or thin-film NM-HEA containing well-mixed noble and less noble metals in a solid solution.
Controlled chemical or electrochemical conditions can selectively dissolve the less noble elements from the NM-HEA.
Mild acidic or alkaline electrolytes under controlled potential are possible dealloying conditions for this process.
Careful control of dealloying time, potential, and current can prevent complete dissolution.
Differences in constituent dissolution rates drive the formation of an interconnected three-dimensional nanoporous framework.
Atoms with lower resistance to oxidation or dissolution are preferentially removed during dealloying.
Preferential atomic removal rearranges the local alloy structure.
Dealloying produces a continuous porous structure enriched in noble metals.
The resulting porous structure increases specific surface area and exposes reactive catalytic sites.
The treated NM-HEA will become a highly porous nanoframework with a noble-metal-enriched catalytic surface.
The dealloyed nanoframework may have higher catalytic efficiency than the undealloyed material.
NM-HEAs made by standard methods such as magnetron sputtering or arc melting typically have relatively dense structures, limited surface area, and less-controlled surface compositions.
Successful framework formation requires sufficient contrast in dissolution rates among the alloy elements.
Insufficient differences in chemical stability can cause unwanted dissolution or collapse of the framework.
Electrolyte concentration, applied potential, and treatment time are critical parameters for controlling dealloying.
